spatial_claims.claim: C is a point on segment AB between A and B, dividing it into AC and CB with AB = AC + CB
CD is a new line segment with CD = 2*AC, C serving as one endpoint
E is a point on segment CD between C and D, cutting CD in extreme and mean ratio with CE as the greater segment and ED as the lesser
13.1 applied to CD cut at E: sq(CE + CD/2) = 5*sq(CD/2), requiring E between C and D with CE as greater segment
CD/2 = AC as a length equality (from CD = 2*AC), substituted into the 13.1 result
CE + AC = AB as a length equality derived from equal squares on positive straight lines
CE = CB derived algebraically from CE + AC = AB and CB = AB - AC

configuration_map: Two independent linear configurations: (1) Line AB with interior point C creating segments AC and CB. (2) Line CD (length 2*AC) with interior point E creating segments CE (greater) and ED (lesser) via extreme and mean ratio. The configurations share point C but never interact spatially -- only their lengths are compared algebraically. No angles, no circles, no interior/exterior relationships are involved.
pass_reason: The proof is fundamentally algebraic. The only spatial claims are that C lies between A and B, and E lies between C and D -- two independent point-on-segment configurations that never interact spatially. All reasoning proceeds through length identities (13.1 applied as a length relationship, algebraic substitution, equal squares implying equal lengths). There are no angle decompositions, no interior/exterior arguments, no ray orderings, and no circle-based reasoning. All spatial claims are trivially consistent.
